trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, a multi-year project replacing low-lying boardwalk sections (B, D, and F) with a higher, sturdier deck began in January 2026 and was expected to finish by summer 2026 — check the park's current conditions page for any remaining rolling detours before you go.
trails.didYouKnow: The boardwalk winds through one of the tallest and most intact old-growth bottomland hardwood forests left in North America.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; driest and most reliably open Sep-Nov
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, low sections of this loop flood roughly ten times a year and can close without notice after heavy rain — check current conditions before setting out.
trails.didYouKnow: Weston Lake is an oxbow lake, a former bend of the Congaree River that was cut off and left behind as the river shifted course.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this backcountry loop crosses low floodplain that can flood after heavy rain — check current conditions and wear waterproof boots even in dry weather.
trails.didYouKnow: Oakridge Trail passes through stands of loblolly pine and mixed hardwood that were never logged, some among the tallest trees in the eastern U.S.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this is the longest and most flood-prone trail in the park — check current conditions before attempting it and be ready to turn back if the floodplain is inundated.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail follows the Congaree River for miles through cypress-tupelo sloughs that can look completely different from one season to the next depending on water levels.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this connector crosses cypress sloughs that flood after heavy rain — check current conditions, since sections can be impassable without notice.
trails.didYouKnow: Despite the name, the trail is more about scenery than snakes — it's named for the Eastern kingsnake, a nonvenomous species known for preying on venomous snakes.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this low-lying connector floods along with the rest of the non-elevated boardwalk system — check current conditions before relying on it as a loop shortcut.
trails.didYouKnow: Sims Trail follows an old fire road and is one of the few trails in the park wide enough for two hikers to walk side by side the whole way.

trails.trailTip: This loop stays on the bluff above the floodplain, making it one of the few trails in the park that reliably stays open and dry even after heavy rain.
trails.didYouKnow: The Bluff Trail runs through drier upland forest rather than floodplain, so its tree mix — more oak and pine — looks noticeably different from the boardwalk's bottomland hardwoods.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this remote loop crosses cypress-tupelo swamp that floods after heavy rain — check current conditions, since this is one of the least-trafficked and least-monitored trails in the park.
trails.didYouKnow: Fork Swamp is a favorite of birders for its dense population of prothonotary warblers, which nest in cavities over standing water.

animals.bestSeason: Year-round; most vocal Feb-Apr during breeding season
animals.whereToLook: Dense old-growth canopy along the Boardwalk Loop and Weston Lake Loop
animals.viewingTip: Listen for its 'who-cooks-for-you' call at dusk and scan the canopy with binoculars rather than using a recorded call to draw it in, which can stress a territorial pair during nesting season.
animals.didYouKnow: Barred owls thrive in Congaree's tall, cavity-rich old growth, which offers far more nesting hollows than younger managed forest.

animals.whereToLook: Floodplain forest edges throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: During the fall rut, watch from a distance with binoculars and give bucks extra space — a rutting buck is more agitated and less predictable than usual, and crowding it can trigger a defensive charge.
animals.didYouKnow: Congaree's deer regularly wade through standing floodwater to reach forage, something rarely seen in upland deer populations.

animals.whereToLook: Cedar Creek and the Congaree River, especially from the Cedar Creek canoe trail
animals.viewingTip: Paddle or watch quietly from the bank with binoculars — otters are naturally curious but will vanish quickly if you move or speak loudly, so patience works better than trying to get close.
animals.didYouKnow: River otters use the same latrine sites repeatedly, so a patch of matted grass and tracks along a creek bank is often a good sign one is active nearby.

animals.whereToLook: Forest floor along the Bluff Trail and Sims Trail
animals.viewingTip: Stay still and quiet if you spot a flock — turkeys are wary and will move off into cover on their own if you don't approach or try to follow them.
animals.didYouKnow: Wild turkeys can fly in short bursts up to 55 mph, despite spending most of their time foraging on the ground.

animals.whereToLook: Sloughs and still water near the boardwalk and Weston Lake
animals.viewingTip: If you see one basking or swimming, give it several feet of space and let it move off on its own — never attempt to handle, corner, or move a cottonmouth, since defensive bites almost always happen when a snake is provoked.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite their reputation, cottonmouths rarely act aggressively toward people and will usually retreat or stand their ground rather than pursue a hiker.

animals.whereToLook: Old-growth trees throughout the boardwalk and backcountry trails
animals.viewingTip: Listen for its loud, irregular drumming and follow the sound with binoculars rather than approaching the tree directly, which can flush the bird before you get a good look.
animals.didYouKnow: The rectangular excavation holes pileated woodpeckers leave in dead wood are so distinctive that other species, from owls to flying squirrels, later move in and use them as nest cavities.

animals.whereToLook: Dense understory away from the main boardwalk, especially near Oakridge and Fork Swamp
animals.viewingTip: Bobcats are rarely seen and quick to disappear into cover — if you spot one, stay put and watch with binoculars rather than following it off-trail.
animals.didYouKnow: Bobcat sightings in Congaree are usually a fresh track in mud rather than the animal itself, since they're largely nocturnal and avoid open trails during the day.

animals.whereToLook: Logs and snags in Weston Lake and other still water
animals.viewingTip: View basking turtles from the boardwalk or shore with binoculars — approaching the water's edge will send them diving off their log before you get a good look.
animals.didYouKnow: Yellow-bellied sliders often stack up several turtles deep on a single favored basking log.
